turns.content: hey, can i ask you something kind of weird? last night i had dinner with my friend tariq to celebrate him getting a job after months of looking. i was genuinely happy for him. but when i finally mentioned my dad's heart surgery next week he literally pulled out his phone in the middle of my sentence to check a fantasy trade and then changed the subject to his gym stipend. am i crazy for feeling like that was messed up? i don't know if i'm overreacting because he was just excited about his job or if this is actually a sign i should stop putting so much into this friendship

You're not crazy. Your dad having heart surgery next week is a genuinely heavy thing to carry, and being cut off mid-sentence for a fantasy trade is a real moment of feeling unseen — especially when you'd just spent the evening celebrating him. That sting makes sense.

That said, I'd be careful about what one dinner proves. A few things worth separating:

**What actually happened:** He was distracted and self-focused at a moment that mattered to you. That's a real miss, and you're allowed to be bothered by it.

**What you don't know yet:** Whether it was one bad night — he was riding high on good news, maybe a little self-absorbed in the moment — or a pattern. The question that matters more: does Tariq usually show up when things are hard for you, or does the friendship mostly run in one direction? One instance of insensitivity is a data point. A habit of it is a signal.

**What I'd actually do:** Say something, rather than quietly recalibrating or pulling away. Something simple and non-accusatory, like: "Hey, the other night when I was telling you about my dad's surgery and you checked your phone — that stung. This one's scary for me and I wanted your support." How he responds will tell you a lot. A friend who says "oh no, I'm sorry, I was being an idiot — how are you doing with it?" is worth the investment. A friend who gets defensive or brushes it off is giving you real information.

On the bigger question — whether to stop putting so much in — I wouldn't decide that from one dinner. Decide it from how he handles being told he hurt you, and from an honest look at whether the support flows both ways over time.

And separately from all the friendship analysis: I hope your dad's surgery goes well. That's a stressful week to be heading into, and it's reasonable to want people around you who can sit with you in it.

yeah i get what you're saying about not deciding from one dinner. and i know tariq isn't a bad guy. but here's the thing i didn't mention — for the past four months i've been his main support system. like every sunday we'd meet at this coffee shop and i'd just let him vent for hours. i remembered the names of hiring managers he mentioned. i'd text him before interviews. i literally stopped complaining about my own stressful job because i didn't want to weigh him down. and then last night i get maybe 30 seconds to mention my dad's surgery before he's checking fantasy football. it just felt like all that effort i put in counted for nothing the second i needed something back

That context changes things, and it's worth saying plainly: this isn't one dinner anymore. What you're describing is a four-month pattern where you were consistently, attentively there for him — and when you finally needed the same thing back, you got 30 seconds before a fantasy trade took priority. Feeling like that effort counted for nothing isn't oversensitivity. It's an accurate read of an imbalance you've been carrying.

A couple of honest observations, though:

**You partly built this.** Not the imbalance itself — that's on him — but the silence around it. You stopped mentioning your own stress to protect him, which meant he may genuinely have no idea you needed anything. People can be self-absorbed without being cruel, and a friend who's never been asked for support sometimes doesn't notice the friendship is lopsided. That doesn't excuse the phone thing mid-sentence about your dad — that's just poor behavior — but it does mean he may not know how one-sided things have become.

**The Sunday coffee shop detail is the real tell.** Hours of venting every week, you remembering hiring managers' names, pre-interview texts — that's real investment. The question isn't whether he's a bad guy. It's whether he's capable of reciprocity once it's named. Some genuinely good people are just oblivious until confronted with it. Others take and take.

So my recommendation stands, but with more weight behind it: tell him directly, and be more explicit than "that stung." Something like: "I've spent four months supporting you through the job search, and I was glad to do it. But last night I needed five minutes about my dad and I didn't get it. I need to know this friendship goes both ways." Then watch what he does — not just what he says. Does he apologize and actually ask about your dad? Does he show up this week, when it actually matters? Or does he deflect?

You don't have to decide today whether to pull back. But you do have to stop protecting him from knowing what you need. The friendship can't be balanced while you're absorbing all the weight silently.

And seriously — with your dad's surgery next week, you deserve people who can hold space for you. If Tariq steps up after being told, great. If he doesn't, you'll have your answer, and it'll be based on something solid.

yeah i think you're right that i need to actually say something instead of just fuming about it. but i'm scared to bring it up because what if he just apologizes and then goes right back to being the same way? or what if he gets defensive and i lose the friendship entirely? we've been close since college and i don't know if i want to risk that over one bad night even if it really hurt

Those fears are reasonable, and I don't want to wave them off — but let me push on the logic of both a little.

**On "what if he apologizes and nothing changes":** That's a real possibility, but notice that it's not a reason to stay silent — it's actually the information you need. If you never say anything, you're guaranteed to stay in the current arrangement: you giving, him receiving, you quietly resenting it. The status quo you're trying to protect is already the thing hurting you. An apology followed by no change isn't a worse outcome than silence; it's the same imbalance, but now you know it's a choice he's making, not an oversight. That clarity is worth having before you decide how much to invest going forward.

**On "what if he gets defensive and I lose the friendship":** A few things. First, a close friendship since college that can't survive one honest, non-hostile conversation about feeling unsupported was already more fragile than it looked. Second, you're not attacking him — you're telling him something true and giving him a chance to fix it. Most decent people, even defensive ones initially, come around within a few days once the sting wears off. And third, notice the asymmetry in what you're risking: you've been carrying this friendship's emotional load for four months, and you're afraid to ask for five minutes about your dad's heart surgery. The thing you'd be "risking the friendship over" is asking it to be slightly mutual. If that's genuinely a friendship-ending request, that's a fact about the friendship, not a mistake you made.

A few practical things that lower the stakes:

- **Don't do it in the heat of a moment or over text if you can avoid it.** A calm, in-person or phone conversation reads as caring, not as an ambush.
- **Lead with the good.** "You're one of my closest friends and I've loved being there for you through the job search" is true, and it frames the conversation as repair, not indictment.
- **Keep it about one specific night, not a four-month indictment.** "When I was telling you about my dad's surgery and you checked your phone, I felt really alone" lands better than a list of grievances, even though the list is legitimate. If he responds well, the bigger pattern can come up naturally.
- **Give him a concrete ask.** "This week is going to be rough and I'd really like you to check in on me" — something specific he can actually do, rather than a vague request to "be more supportive."

One more thing, gently: you spent four months muting your own needs to avoid weighing him down. Being scared to bring this up is the same instinct in a new form. The cost of that instinct is that you end up alone with the hard stuff — which is exactly where you found yourself last night. You don't have to stop being a giving friend. You just have to let the friendship include you too.

Whatever happens with Tariq, I hope the surgery goes well and that you've got people around you this week.

i think i've been sitting here for like 20 minutes trying to draft a text to him and i keep deleting it. part of me wants to just send "hey remember when i told you my dad needs heart surgery and you checked your phone? that was shitty" and be done with it. but i also know that's just gonna blow everything up and i'll regret it

Twenty minutes of deleting drafts tells you something real: you care about this friendship and you don't want to torch it. That instinct is worth trusting over the "that was shitty" impulse — not because your anger is wrong, but because a text like that starts a fight instead of a conversation, and then you get defensiveness instead of finding out whether he can actually show up for you.

Here's a draft you could adapt:

> "Hey — can I be honest about something from last night? When I was telling you about my dad's surgery and you checked your phone, it really stung. I've been glad to be there for you through the whole job search, and I don't regret any of it. But this week is going to be hard for me and I need you in my corner too. Can we talk?"

Why this works:

- **It names the specific moment** without characterizing him ("that was shitty" makes him the villain; "it stung" makes it your honest experience — much harder to argue with).
- **It acknowledges the good history**, so he doesn't hear it as an attack on four months of friendship.
- **It makes a concrete ask** — talk, and show up this week — instead of just venting.
- **It's short.** Long texts invite long defensive replies. Short texts invite a conversation.

A couple of practical notes: send it when you're not freshly angry (you seem past that now, which is good), and don't send it at a time when he's obviously busy or it'll sit unanswered for hours — that'll just feed the anxiety while you wait.

One thing to brace for: he might respond awkwardly or a little defensively at first. That's okay. What matters is what he does over the next few days — whether he calls, asks about your dad, checks in during the week. Judge the response by actions, not the first text back.

You've got the harder part done already, which is deciding to say it at all. The draft is just delivery.
yeah i think that draft is good but i don't know if i can send it tonight. i'm still too angry honestly. maybe i just need to sleep on it and see how i feel tomorrow before i say anything permanent

That's a sound call, and honestly the right one. Sending it while you're still angry is exactly the scenario you were trying to avoid — the message might be fine, but you'd be sending it from a place where you're not steady yet, and you'd likely be refreshing your phone all night waiting for a reply you might not like.

A few things to make sleeping on it actually work:

- **Set a rough time to revisit it tomorrow** — like mid-morning or afternoon — so "sleep on it" doesn't quietly become "never send it." You've already decided to say something; you're just choosing when. That's different from backing out.
- **Re-read the draft tomorrow before sending, but don't rewrite it much.** Tomorrow-you will be calmer, which is good for tone-checking, but also more prone to softening it into nothing or talking yourself out of it entirely. If it still feels honest and fair tomorrow, send it as-is.
- **Notice the anger itself.** It's not a problem to fix before the conversation — it's information. It's telling you how much this mattered. You can send a calm message *and* still be angry underneath; those aren't in conflict.

And one small thing: if tomorrow comes and you're still too worked up, that's fine too — this doesn't have a deadline. What matters is that it doesn't get buried. The version to avoid isn't "sent it a day later than planned," it's "never said anything and let the resentment calcify."

Sleep on it. You've done the hard thinking already.
